title: HELL IS REAL… BUT YOU WERE NEVER CREATED FOR IT
paragraphs:
HELL IS REAL… BUT YOU WERE NEVER CREATED FOR IT
The Terrifying Truth Most People Avoid, The Mercy Most People Miss, And The Savior Who Stood Between You and Eternal Judgment
There is a reason why conversations about Hell make people uncomfortable.
Not because Hell is fictional.
Not because Hell is outdated.
Not because Jesus avoided talking about it.
But because deep inside every human soul exists a terrifying awareness that eternity is real.
You can silence it.
You can distract yourself from it.
You can laugh at it.
You can argue against it.
But when the room becomes quiet enough, when the noise fades, when life suddenly breaks your heart, when death unexpectedly visits someone you love, the question returns.
What happens after this?
The modern world has become remarkably skilled at discussing almost everything except eternity.
We debate politics.
We analyze culture.
We obsess over success.
We chase money.
We pursue pleasure.
Yet many refuse to ask the one question that matters most:
What if Jesus was telling the truth about Hell?
That question changes everything.
Because according to Scripture, Hell was never invented by angry preachers.
It was described by Jesus Himself.
And what makes that reality even more shocking is this:
The same Jesus who spoke most powerfully about God's love also spoke more about Hell than anyone else in the Bible.
Not because He wanted people terrified.
Because He wanted people rescued.
The Bible's understanding of Hell cannot be separated from the holiness of God.
In Hebrew thought, God is not merely good.
He is holy.
The Hebrew word is קָדוֹשׁ (qadosh).
It means set apart, utterly pure, morally perfect, completely separated from evil.
Isaiah encountered this reality when heavenly beings cried:
"Holy, holy, holy is the LORD of hosts; the whole earth is full of his glory." (Isaiah 6:3)
Notice they did not say loving, loving, loving.
Powerful, powerful, powerful.
Merciful, merciful, merciful.
Though God is all those things.
The only attribute repeated three times is holy.
When Isaiah encountered that holiness, he did not celebrate himself.
He collapsed.
"Woe is me! For I am lost." (Isaiah 6:5)
For the first time he saw himself accurately.
And that is where understanding Hell begins.
Not with God's cruelty.
But with God's holiness.
Most people compare themselves to other sinners.
"I am not that bad."
"I am better than most."
"I've never killed anyone."
"I try to be a good person."
Yet Scripture never uses humanity as the measuring stick.
The standard is God Himself.
Romans 3:23 says:
"For all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God."
All.
Not some.
Not the especially wicked.
Not only criminals.
All.
The Greek word for sin is ἁμαρτία (hamartia).
It literally means missing the mark.
Every lie.
Every selfish motive.
Every hidden thought.
Every act of rebellion.
Every moment we placed ourselves on the throne instead of God.
Sin is not merely breaking rules.
It is rejecting the rightful King.
And if God is infinitely holy, then rebellion against Him carries eternal consequences.
This is where many people struggle.
How can a loving God allow Hell?
The better question may be:
How can a perfectly holy God allow sinners into His presence without justice?
Because if evil never faces judgment, then justice becomes meaningless.
Every victim cries out for justice.
Every abused child.
Every exploited person.
Every murdered innocent.
Every betrayed heart.
Deep inside us is a longing for wrongs to be made right.
That longing exists because justice originates from God Himself.
The Bible describes Hell using several words.
One Hebrew term is שְׁאוֹל (Sheol), often referring to the realm of the dead.
In Greek, the New Testament frequently uses ᾅδης (Hades), referring to the place of the dead.
But perhaps the most sobering term Jesus used was γέεννα (Gehenna).
Gehenna referred to the Valley of Hinnom outside Jerusalem.
Historically it became associated with judgment, corruption, and destruction.
Jesus deliberately used this image to communicate the horror of eternal separation from God.
In Mark 9:43 Jesus warned:
"It is better for you to enter life crippled than with two hands to go to hell, to the unquenchable fire."
Notice something important.
Jesus never softened Hell.
He never apologized for it.
He never treated it as symbolic nonsense.
He spoke about it because He loved people enough to warn them.
Imagine seeing a bridge collapsed ahead while people drive toward it.
Love warns.
Love speaks.
Love refuses silence.
That is exactly what Jesus was doing.
Yet Hell is not merely about fire.
The deepest horror is separation.
2 Thessalonians 1:9 says people will be:
"away from the presence of the Lord and from the glory of his might."
Think carefully about that.
Every good thing humans enjoy ultimately flows from God.
Love.
Beauty.
Joy.
Peace.
Purpose.
Hope.
Truth.
Meaning.
Hell represents the complete and eternal absence of those blessings.
The separation humanity insisted upon becomes permanent.
C.S. Lewis once summarized the reality by explaining that people ultimately say either "Thy will be done" to God, or God says "thy will be done" to them.
Hell is the final consequence of choosing life apart from God.
Yet if the story ended there, Christianity would be the most hopeless message ever told.
But this is where the Gospel explodes into history.
Because while humanity deserved judgment, God chose rescue.
John 3:16 is quoted often, but rarely do people continue reading.
"For God so loved the world, that he gave his only Son, that whoever believes in him should not perish but have eternal life."
Notice the contrast.
Perish.
Or eternal life.
Judgment.
Or salvation.
Hell.
Or Heaven.
The Gospel does not deny Hell.
The Gospel provides escape from Hell.
And that escape came at a price beyond comprehension.
On the cross Jesus experienced what no sinner could survive.
The innocent Son stood where the guilty belonged.
Isaiah 53:5 says:
"But he was pierced for our transgressions; he was crushed for our iniquities."
The Greek word τετέλεσται (tetelestai), spoken by Jesus in John 19:30, means:
"It is finished."
Paid in full.
Completed.
The debt satisfied.
Justice fulfilled.
Mercy released.
At Calvary, God did not ignore sin.
He judged sin.
But He judged it in Christ.
This is why Christianity is unlike every other religion.
The message is not:
Work harder.
Become better.
Earn forgiveness.
The message is:
Jesus paid what you could never pay.
Jesus carried what you could never carry.
Jesus endured what you deserved.
So you could receive what you never deserved.
Grace.
The theme of Scripture has always been scandal to grace.
A murderer named Moses becomes a deliverer.
An adulterer named David becomes a king after God's heart.
A prostitute named Rahab becomes part of the Messiah's lineage.
A persecutor named Saul becomes the Apostle Paul.
A thief dying on a cross enters Paradise.
Every one of them proves the same truth.
Jesus rewrites everything.
And perhaps that is why Hell matters so much.
Because you cannot understand the magnitude of salvation until you understand what Christ saved us from.
The cross only appears small when judgment appears small.
But when we see the reality of eternal separation, the sacrifice of Jesus becomes infinitely precious.
Maybe someone reading this has spent years pretending.
Religious on the outside.
Broken on the inside.
Maybe you have hidden sins nobody knows.
Maybe shame has convinced you that you are beyond redemption.
Maybe your scandal feels bigger than God's grace.
It is not.
The cross already settled that argument.
The empty tomb settled it permanently.
Hell is real.
Judgment is real.
Eternity is real.
But so is grace.
So is forgiveness.
So is redemption.
So is Jesus.
And right now, if your heart feels convicted, that is not an accident.
That may be the mercy of God reaching for you.
Be honest.
This hit harder than you expected.
One day every excuse will disappear, every argument will fall silent, every secret will be revealed, and only one question will matter: What did you do with Jesus Christ?
